title: Sticking with it until it's finished
keyIdea: Sticking with it means you choose a job, like a jigsaw, a drawing or a tower, and keep going until it is all done. Nearly done is not finished: look closely for any missing part. You can stop for snack or sleep, leave the job safe and come back to finish it. A big job gets done one small bit at a time. When it is done, say "I finished it!", show someone and feel proud.

kid: You pick a jigsaw. You put in one piece, then more. Is it done? Not yet! It is done when every piece is in. The last piece is the best one.
Look closely before you say done. Does the face have two eyes? Does the car have all its wheels? If a bit is missing, add it.
Sometimes we stop. It is snack time, or bath time. Leave your tower safe. Then come back and add the top block.
A big picture has lots of bits. Do one bit. Then one more. When it is all done, say: I finished it! Then show a grown-up.
adult: This is task persistence, one of the approaches to learning in early years frameworks. The EYFS framework names active learning as a characteristic of effective learning. Children concentrate, keep on trying and enjoy what they achieve. The Head Start framework lists persistence in tasks under approaches to learning. At 3 to 4 years the aim is to follow a short job they chose through to the end, and to know when it is done.

Three skills sit underneath. Checking for completion: young children often call a job done when it is mostly done, so teach them to look for the missing part. Resuming: a pause is not the end. Keeping the work safe and coming back to it builds the habit of finishing. Chunking: a long job feels possible when it is split into small bits you can see, like one row of the jigsaw or one colour at a time.

Common mistakes: finishing the job for the child because it is quicker, which takes away the finish; picking tasks that are far too big, such as a 48-piece jigsaw for a 3-year-old; packing work away at tidy-up time so there is nothing to come back to; and praising cleverness rather than effort. Be careful with praise. Name the process: you kept going until the last piece was in.

In the lab your child drags every jigsaw piece home and spots what a picture still needs. They leave a tower safe at snack time and come back to finish it. They colour a long caterpillar one part at a time while a bar fills. Then they practise the finish: last bit, say I finished it, show it.

familyTip: Keep a 'not finished yet' shelf. When a jigsaw or drawing has to stop for dinner, put it there together, then bring it out the next day so your child can finish it and say, 'I finished it!'

visual.caption: Is it finished yet? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Tower with its top block on

lab.caption: Flagship lab: put in every jigsaw piece, spot what is missing, come back to a tower after snack, colour bit by bit and say I finished it.

practice.prompt: Sticking with it: Mia's jigsaw has one piece left and she wants to stop. Is her jigsaw finished?
practice.hint: A jigsaw is finished when every single piece is in. Count the gaps.
practice.explain: There is still one gap, so it is not finished yet. One more piece and Mia can say: I finished it!

practice.prompt: A jigsaw has {n} pieces. {k} pieces are in. How many more pieces until it is finished?
practice.hint: Count on from {k} to {n}, one piece at a time.
practice.explain: From {k} pieces to {n} pieces is {=n-k} more pieces, then the jigsaw is finished.

practice.prompt: It is snack time and Leo's tower is not finished. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Leave it safe and come back after snack
practice.hint: Think about what lets Leo finish his tower later.
practice.explain: If he leaves it safe, the tower waits for him. After snack he can add the top block and finish it.

practice.prompt: Sam builds a tower of {n} blocks, then stops for lunch and leaves it safe. After lunch, how many blocks are still in the tower?
practice.hint: Nobody knocked it down. Leaving it safe means nothing changes.
practice.explain: The tower still has {n} blocks, so Sam can carry on from {n} and finish it.

pool.prompt: A drawing of a car has only 3 wheels. Is it finished?
pool.hint: Look closely. How many wheels does a car have?
pool.explain: A car has 4 wheels, so one is missing. Add the last wheel, then the car is finished.

pool.prompt: Your big picture has lots of parts to colour. What helps you finish it?
choices: Colour one part at a time
pool.hint: A big job is lots of little bits.
pool.explain: One part, then the next, then the next. Little bits add up until the whole picture is finished.

pool.prompt: A caterpillar has {n} parts to colour. You have coloured {k}. How many parts are left?
pool.hint: Take the coloured parts away from all the parts.
pool.explain: {n} parts take away {k} coloured is {=n-k} left to colour, then it is finished.

pool.prompt: Ava finished her jigsaw. What can she do now?
choices: Say I finished it and show someone
pool.hint: Finishing feels good. Who would like to see it?
pool.explain: She can say: I finished it! Showing a grown-up lets her feel proud of sticking with it.

pool.prompt: Ben stopped his drawing yesterday. What can he do today?
choices: Start a new one and forget it
pool.hint: A pause is not the end of a job.
pool.explain: Ben can take out his drawing and finish the last bits. Coming back counts as sticking with it.

pool.prompt: A tower needs {n} blocks to reach the top. It has {k} blocks now. How many more blocks?
pool.explain: {k} blocks plus {=n-k} more blocks makes {n}, so the tower needs {=n-k} more to be finished.

pool.hint: Look for gaps. Are there any left?
pool.explain: A jigsaw is finished only when there are no gaps. Most pieces is not all pieces.

pool.prompt: A face drawing has one eye. What does it need to be finished?
pool.hint: How many eyes does a face have?
pool.explain: A face has two eyes, so it needs one more eye. Then the drawing is finished.
